body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"A pre-assessment insulin dose-adjustment plan and day-of-surgery glucose: a before-after study","authors":"Ferreira-Mensah D, Holloway-Iwu K, Lindgren-Obasi T","year":2022,"venue":"Perioperative Medicine Reports","doi":"10.5555/pmr.2022.0187","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We introduced a written insulin dose-adjustment plan, handed to patients at pre-assessment, for adults with insulin-treated diabetes having elective surgery, and compared 214 patients after the change with 198 before. Out-of-range glucose on the day of surgery, defined as a capillary value above 12 or below 4 mmol/L, fell from 34 percent to 21 percent. Use of variable-rate insulin infusions fell from 46 to 18 percent of patients. Hypoglycaemia in the 24 hours after surgery was similar (6 against 5 percent). The comparison was uncontrolled, and staff awareness of the evaluation may have changed practice beyond the plan itself."},{"title":"Specialist nurse telephone contact before elective surgery for people with insulin-treated diabetes: a pilot randomised trial","authors":"Adeyemi-Castell R, Nakashima-Doyle F","year":2020,"venue":"Journal of Perioperative Diabetes Care","doi":"10.5555/jpdc.2020.0034","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"We randomised 60 adults with insulin-treated diabetes to a diabetes specialist nurse phone call two days before elective surgery or to usual care. Recruitment was 48 percent of eligible patients, meeting the progression criterion of 40 percent, and 94 percent of intervention patients received the call. Out-of-range glucose on the day of surgery occurred in 30 percent of intervention and 43 percent of usual-care patients, an imprecise difference. Outcome data were complete for 79 percent, below the 90 percent criterion, mainly because capillary values were not documented on the ward. The authors did not proceed to a definitive trial."},{"title":"First-on-the-list scheduling for patients with diabetes: feasibility across surgical specialties","authors":"Oyelaran-Whitby S, Kaur-Brandt M","year":2019,"venue":"Theatre Operations Research","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We measured how often adults with diabetes could be scheduled first on the morning operating list in three hospitals over one year. First-on-the-list scheduling was achieved for 71 percent of general surgery patients, 38 percent of orthopaedic patients and 64 percent of urology patients. Orthopaedic lists were often reordered for implant availability and trauma. When achieved, fasting time fell by a mean of 3.1 hours. Surgeons and theatre managers supported the principle but reported that it competed with other scheduling priorities such as children and patients with latex allergy."},{"title":"Subcutaneous correction scales versus variable-rate insulin infusion for short elective operations: a cohort study","authors":"Brennan-Achterberg L, Moyo-Hartmann J, Silva-Okafor N","year":2023,"venue":"Perioperative Medicine Reports","doi":"10.5555/pmr.2023.0042","providerType":"cohort","abstract":"In 1,020 elective operations lasting under three hours in adults with insulin-treated diabetes, we compared patients managed with a subcutaneous insulin correction scale with those started on a variable-rate intravenous insulin infusion. Hypoglycaemia below 4 mmol/L within 24 hours occurred in 4 percent with the correction scale and 9 percent with the infusion. Hyperglycaemia above 12 mmol/L was similar in both groups. Patients started on an infusion were older and had longer operations, so confounding by indication is likely. Infusions continued for more than 24 hours in 31 percent of infusion patients."},{"title":"Perioperative hyperglycaemia and surgical site infection in patients with diabetes: a systematic review","authors":"Tanaka-Ruiz E, Obi-Lindahl C, Graves-Mbatha P, Holm-Adebayo R","year":2021,"venue":"Surgical Infection Reviews","doi":"10.5555/sir.2021.0290","providerType":"review","abstract":"We searched four databases to 2020 for studies of perioperative glucose and surgical site infection in adults with diabetes. Nineteen studies met the criteria, most of them observational. Glucose above 10 to 12 mmol/L around the time of surgery was associated with higher odds of surgical site infection (pooled odds ratio 1.8, 95 percent CI 1.4 to 2.3), with moderate heterogeneity. Thresholds and timing of glucose measurement varied between studies. Two small trials of tighter perioperative control did not show a clear reduction in infection, and one reported more hypoglycaemia."},{"title":"Patients' experience of conflicting diabetes instructions before surgery: a qualitative study","authors":"Lindqvist-Oduya M, Fairweather-Nkemelu A","year":2024,"venue":"Patient Experience in Surgery","providerType":"qualitative","abstract":"We spoke with 22 adults with insulin-treated diabetes after elective surgery about the instructions they had received. Most described receiving different advice about their insulin from the pre-assessment clinic, the surgical team and the ward. Several reduced or stopped insulin on their own because they feared low glucose while fasting. Participants valued a single written plan that all staff followed and a named person to call. Patients who had surgery late in the day described the longest periods of uncertainty. Participants were recruited from one hospital."},{"title":"Capillary glucose meter accuracy in the perioperative period","authors":"Kowalczyk-Adeyemi B, Haldane-Tan S","year":2016,"venue":"Clinical Laboratory Practice","doi":"10.5555/clp.2016.0118","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared 410 paired capillary meter and laboratory glucose values in surgical patients before, during and after operations. Above 5.5 mmol/L, 95 percent of meter values were within 15 percent of the laboratory value. Below 4 mmol/L, agreement was poorer and meters tended to read high, which could delay recognition of hypoglycaemia. Low haematocrit after blood loss increased the meter bias. The authors recommend laboratory confirmation of low meter values and caution when meters are the only measure of hypoglycaemia in perioperative studies."}]}
